## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

1	# Repository templates — the catalog
2	
3	> DevDesk architecture notes. Referenced from `.claude/CLAUDE.md`;
4	> read this file when working on the code it describes.
5	
6	`internal/template` is the catalog of templates a new repository can be filled
7	from, and how their files are fetched. `internal/ui/templates` is the
8	`:templates` view over it (below). The picker in the creation form comes later;
9	the plan is `.claude/plans/2026-09-18-repo-templates.md`.
10	
11	## An entry is a reference
12	
13	An `Entry` holds a slug, a name, a description, tags and a `Source`. The content
14	stays where it is and is fetched when a repository is created from it, so a
15	template cannot drift from its original.
16	
17	| `Source.Kind` | `URL` | `Path` | `Ref` |
18	|---|---|---|---|
19	| `git` | clone URL | optional subdirectory, made the root | branch, tag or SHA |
20	| `local` | — | repository directory | branch, tag or SHA |
21	| `oci` | registry URL | repository | tag |
22	
23	The catalog is **global**: `~/.devdesk/templates.yaml`, not one per context.
24	Every entry is declared. There used to be a second source, entries listed from a
25	registry's `/v2/_catalog` and merged in; it was removed because nobody used it,
26	and an OCI template is declared by hand like any other. `registry.templates_repository`
27	is therefore read by nothing and stays in the schema only so existing files
28	still load.
29	
30	## Fetching
31	
32	`Fetch(ctx, src, Credentials)` returns `[]File{Path, Content []byte, Executable}`.
33	
34	- **git and local both go through `git archive`.** What comes back is what was
35	  *committed*: no `.git`, nothing ignored, no uncommitted edit — a template must
36	  not depend on someone's working tree. A directory that is not a repository is
37	  refused, not copied raw. `.gitattributes export-ignore` is honoured, which is
38	  git's own answer to "what is part of a release".
39	- **git remote** is `init` + `fetch --depth 1 <ref>` + `archive FETCH_HEAD`, in a
40	  temp directory removed before returning. `clone --branch` would refuse a SHA,
41	  and a template pinned to a SHA is the reproducible kind. Nothing is cached yet:
42	  `F` (sync) in the view is what will own a cache.
43	- **oci** reuses `oci.Client.DownloadTemplate`, which returns `Entries`
44	  (bytes + execute bit).
45	- A symlink in a template is **refused**, naming it and saying to replace it
46	  with a regular file. It used to be read as an empty file — a template silently
47	  missing what it says it holds. A **submodule** is refused the same way
48	  (`git ls-tree` finds the gitlink): `git archive` writes it as an empty
49	  directory, which would be the same silent gap.
50	
51	**Credentials are resolved per host** by `CredentialsFor(cfg, secrets, src)`: the
52	forge's token goes only to a git source on the forge's host, the registry's
53	password only to an OCI source on the registry's, and anything else is fetched
54	anonymously — a token authenticates one host, and the catalog can be shared, so
55	the entry cannot be what decides. Nothing is sent over `http://` either, even to
56	the forge's own host. A private repository on any other host is not
57	reachable over HTTPS: use an SSH URL. Both the view and the explorer call it, so
58	the rule has one place to live.
59	
60	**A template has limits: 500 files and 32 MiB** (`MaxFiles`, `MaxBytes`),
61	checked inside `Fetch` and so before anything is created on the forge. They are
62	enforced **while reading**, not after: `git archive`'s output is capped
63	(`git.ErrOutputTooLarge`) and the tar/gzip readers stop at the limits
64	(`oci.Limits`, `oci.ErrArchiveTooLarge`), so a huge repository or a gzip bomb
65	is never held in memory whole. `checkLimits` still names the biggest file for
66	what got that far. GitLab
67	takes every file in one request, so the body size decides; GitHub takes one
68	request per file, one after the other, so the count does. The numbers are
69	estimates: the one to verify against a real GitLab instance is its maximum
70	request body, which has to admit 32 MiB once base64-encoded (about 43 MiB).
71	
72	## The catalog file is not trusted
73	
74	It can be shared or hand-edited, so `Entry.Validate` runs on `Put` **and on
75	load**. A bad entry, or a slug declared twice, does not fail `Open`: it is set
76	aside (`Store.Problems()`, reported as a footer warning), the rest of the
77	catalog stays usable, and the entry stays in the file so saving another one
78	does not delete a hand-edited line:
79	
80	- git URLs must be `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git` or scp-form. `ext::` runs a
81	  command and `file://` reads this machine; a checkout on this machine is the
82	  `local` kind precisely so neither is needed.
83	- A URL or ref beginning with `-` is refused — git would read it as an option.
84	  `internal/git` repeats that check, since it is the last stop before `exec`.
85	
86	Writes go to a sibling file renamed over the catalog, and memory only changes if
87	the write succeeded, so a failure leaves both agreeing.
88	
89	## The `:templates` view — `internal/ui/templates`
90	
91	A `datatable` (icon, Name, Tags, Source, Ref) over the catalog. The body is
92	always the table (Rule 139); the count is in the header.
93	
94	| Key | Does |
95	|---|---|
96	| `N` | new entry — form in the viewport (Rule 112), source kind is a `←→` cycle field (Rule 132) |
97	| `E` | edit |
98	| `D` | delete after a confirmation that defaults to No |
99	| `S` | scan the template for vulnerabilities and secrets (below) |
100	| `V` | preview: asks the router to open the viewer on a listing of the files the template would put in a repository (`previewSource`), so a fetch failure is reported by the viewer's own load path |
101	| `.` `/` | sort, filter (name, description, tags, source) |
102	
103	**The slug is derived from the name on creation and fixed on edit.** Renaming a
104	template must not orphan whatever remembered its old slug.
105	
106	**A local source has no URL field**; the same three inputs (`url`, `path`,
107	`ref`) serve every kind and only their labels change, so a value typed before
108	cycling the kind is kept.
109	
110	**An unreadable catalog refuses every write.** Saving over a file that could
111	not be parsed would replace whatever the user had in it; the footer says so and
112	`N`/`E`/`D` are greyed with the reason. The catalog not being *open yet* is not
113	greyed — that is not knowing, and greying it for one read would look like a
114	glitch (Rule 130).
115	
116	## Creating a repository from a template
117	
118	The `Template` field of the explorer's creation form (projects only) shows
119	`none` — an empty repository — until one is chosen.
120	
121	- **`enter` on the field opens the catalog**, lent by the router in selection
122	  mode (`templates.NewForSelection`), the second borrow the explorer makes (see
123	  `scanning.md`). The form is kept as it is meanwhile; `enter` in the picker
124	  answers `TemplateSelectedMsg{Slug, Name}`, `esc` answers
125	  `SelectionCancelledMsg`, and the router turns them into the explorer's own
126	  `TemplateChosenMsg` / `TemplateChoiceCancelledMsg`. `backspace` on the field
127	  puts it back to none.
128	- **The picker is the whole catalog**, filterable and sortable, with `V` to look
129	  inside. N, E and D are not bound there — a mode replaces the list (Rule 130).
130	  The form keeps the slug and shows the name; the slug is what is submitted.
131	- **The template is fetched before the repository is created.** A bad ref, a
132	  network failure, a refused login, a template that is gone from the catalog or
133	  one over the limits all fail with *nothing created*: the footer says so and the
134	  run detail reads `template unavailable — nothing was created`. Only the initial
135	  commit can still fail once the repository exists, and that keeps the old
136	  outcome: the repository stays, empty, and the footer says it was created empty.
137	  The run item is **failed** (`created empty — the template's commit failed`), not
138	  done: what was asked for was a repository with a template in it.
139	- **A create is bounded, not cancellable.** `jobs.Kind.Cancellable` says no for
140	  `create` (a request already sent cannot be un-sent), so the guard against a
141	  stalled forge is a timeout: one minute for the repository, ten for the initial
142	  commit (GitHub makes one request per file).
143	- The catalog is read when the template is applied, not when the form opens, so
144	  a template deleted while the form was open is reported as no longer in the
145	  catalog rather than applied from a stale copy.
146	
147	## Scanning a template
148	
149	A secret in a template ends up in every repository made from it, so `S` scans
150	what the template would put in a repository — before it does.
151	
152	The template is fetched, written to **`~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>`**
153	(`template.Materialize`, which replaces whatever a previous scan left there), and
154	that directory is scanned as a plain directory by the configured scanners. It is
155	reused as a directory scan on purpose: the result is cached by path
156	(`cache.StoreWorkspaceScan`, now shared with the workspaces view), so it appears
157	in the **`:sec` inventory** and opens in the same results view, with nothing new
158	to build. The footer here says how it ended — the counts, or `no findings`, or a
159	warning when a stage failed and found nothing (which is not the same claim). The
160	workspaces list is not involved: the copy is not in it, and nothing pretends it is.
161	
162	- **Fixed directory, not a temp one**, because the scan is cached by path: a
163	  fresh directory per scan would leave a dead `:sec` entry behind for each.
164	- **`Materialize` computes and empties only its own directory.** It takes a slug,
165	  validates it, and derives the path — a caller cannot point the removal
166	  elsewhere — and refuses a file whose path would land outside it.
167	- **No CI score.** A template has no pipeline to grade, and plumber would look
168	  for a remote it does not have.
169	- **It is registry work** (`jobs.KindScan`, origin `:templates`), so `:jobs`
170	  lists it, `K` stops it, and the router stamps the context the counts are stored
171	  under (D68). `ScanStartingMsg` and `ScanCompleteMsg` implement `jobs.Reporter`
172	  and are routed through `routeWork`; a test pins that, because implementing the
173	  interface proves nothing if the router never calls it.
174	- **`S` is greyed** when neither Trivy nor Gitleaks is available, and while a
175	  scan of that template is running (whoever started it). Until the scanner check
176	  comes back it stays lit — greying it for a few frames would read as a glitch
177	  (Rule 130). The picker has no `S`.
178	
179	## Not done yet
180	
181	- `F` (sync) and the cache it would own: every preview, creation and scan
182	  refetches.
183	- A private git repository on a host that is not the forge's is fetched
184	  anonymously, so it fails with git's own reason: use an SSH URL.
185	- No spinner on the row itself: the footer status carries the live scan.

anonymously — a token authenticates one host, and the catalog can be shared, so
the entry cannot be what decides. Nothing is sent over `http://` either, even to
the forge's own host. A private repository on any other host is not
reachable over HTTPS: use an SSH URL. Both the view and the explorer call it, so
the rule has one place to live.

**A template has limits: 500 files and 32 MiB** (`MaxFiles`, `MaxBytes`),
checked inside `Fetch` and so before anything is created on the forge. They are
enforced **while reading**, not after: `git archive`'s output is capped
(`git.ErrOutputTooLarge`) and the tar/gzip readers stop at the limits
(`oci.Limits`, `oci.ErrArchiveTooLarge`), so a huge repository or a gzip bomb
is never held in memory whole. `checkLimits` still names the biggest file for
what got that far. GitLab
takes every file in one request, so the body size decides; GitHub takes one
request per file, one after the other, so the count does. The numbers are
estimates: the one to verify against a real GitLab instance is its maximum
request body, which has to admit 32 MiB once base64-encoded (about 43 MiB).

## The catalog file is not trusted

It can be shared or hand-edited, so `Entry.Validate` runs on `Put` **and on
load**. A bad entry, or a slug declared twice, does not fail `Open`: it is set
aside (`Store.Problems()`, reported as a footer warning), the rest of the
catalog stays usable, and the entry stays in the file so saving another one
does not delete a hand-edited line:

- git URLs must be `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git` or scp-form. `ext::` runs a
  command and `file://` reads this machine; a checkout on this machine is the
  `local` kind precisely so neither is needed.
- A URL or ref beginning with `-` is refused — git would read it as an option.
  `internal/git` repeats that check, since it is the last stop before `exec`.

Writes go to a sibling file renamed over the catalog, and memory only changes if
the write succeeded, so a failure leaves both agreeing.

## The `:templates` view — `internal/ui/templates`

A `datatable` (icon, Name, Tags, Source, Ref) over the catalog. The body is
always the table (Rule 139); the count is in the header.

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| `N` | new entry — form in the viewport (Rule 112), source kind is a `←→` cycle field (Rule 132) |
| `E` | edit |
| `D` | delete after a confirmation that defaults to No |
| `S` | scan the template for vulnerabilities and secrets (below) |
| `V` | preview: asks the router to open the viewer on a listing of the files the template would put in a repository (`previewSource`), so a fetch failure is reported by the viewer's own load path |
| `.` `/` | sort, filter (name, description, tags, source) |

**The slug is derived from the name on creation and fixed on edit.** Renaming a
template must not orphan whatever remembered its old slug.

**A local source has no URL field**; the same three inputs (`url`, `path`,
`ref`) serve every kind and only their labels change, so a value typed before
cycling the kind is kept.

**An unreadable catalog refuses every write.** Saving over a file that could
not be parsed would replace whatever the user had in it; the footer says so and
`N`/`E`/`D` are greyed with the reason. The catalog not being *open yet* is not
greyed — that is not knowing, and greying it for one read would look like a
glitch (Rule 130).

## Creating a repository from a template

The `Template` field of the explorer's creation form (projects only) shows
`none` — an empty repository — until one is chosen.

- **`enter` on the field opens the catalog**, lent by the router in selection
  mode (`templates.NewForSelection`), the second borrow the explorer makes (see
  `scanning.md`). The form is kept as it is meanwhile; `enter` in the picker
  answers `TemplateSelectedMsg{Slug, Name}`, `esc` answers
  `SelectionCancelledMsg`, and the router turns them into the explorer's own
  `TemplateChosenMsg` / `TemplateChoiceCancelledMsg`. `backspace` on the field
  puts it back to none.
- **The picker is the whole catalog**, filterable and sortable, with `V` to look
  inside. N, E and D are not bound there — a mode replaces the list (Rule 130).
  The form keeps the slug and shows the name; the slug is what is submitted.
- **The template is fetched before the repository is created.** A bad ref, a
  network failure, a refused login, a template that is gone from the catalog or
  one over the limits all fail with *nothing created*: the footer says so and the
  run detail reads `template unavailable — nothing was created`. Only the initial
  commit can still fail once the repository exists, and that keeps the old
  outcome: the repository stays, empty, and the footer says it was created empty.
  The run item is **failed** (`created empty — the template's commit failed`), not
  done: what was asked for was a repository with a template in it.
- **A create is bounded, not cancellable.** `jobs.Kind.Cancellable` says no for
  `create` (a request already sent cannot be un-sent), so the guard against a
  stalled forge is a timeout: one minute for the repository, ten for the initial
  commit (GitHub makes one request per file).
- The catalog is read when the template is applied, not when the form opens, so
  a template deleted while the form was open is reported as no longer in the
  catalog rather than applied from a stale copy.

## Scanning a template

A secret in a template ends up in every repository made from it, so `S` scans
what the template would put in a repository — before it does.

The template is fetched, written to **`~/.devdesk/cache/template-scan/<slug>`**
(`template.Materialize`, which replaces whatever a previous scan left there), and
that directory is scanned as a plain directory by the configured scanners. It is
reused as a directory scan on purpose: the result is cached by path
(`cache.StoreWorkspaceScan`, now shared with the workspaces view), so it appears
in the **`:sec` inventory** and opens in the same results view, with nothing new
to build. The footer here says how it ended — the counts, or `no findings`, or a
warning when a stage failed and found nothing (which is not the same claim). The
workspaces list is not involved: the copy is not in it, and nothing pretends it is.

- **Fixed directory, not a temp one**, because the scan is cached by path: a
  fresh directory per scan would leave a dead `:sec` entry behind for each.
- **`Materialize` computes and empties only its own directory.** It takes a slug,
  validates it, and derives the path — a caller cannot point the removal
  elsewhere — and refuses a file whose path would land outside it.
- **No CI score.** A template has no pipeline to grade, and plumber would look
  for a remote it does not have.
- **It is registry work** (`jobs.KindScan`, origin `:templates`), so `:jobs`
  lists it, `K` stops it, and the router stamps the context the counts are stored
  under (D68). `ScanStartingMsg` and `ScanCompleteMsg` implement `jobs.Reporter`
  and are routed through `routeWork`; a test pins that, because implementing the
  interface proves nothing if the router never calls it.
- **`S` is greyed** when neither Trivy nor Gitleaks is available, and while a
  scan of that template is running (whoever started it). Until the scanner check
  comes back it stays lit — greying it for a few frames would read as a glitch
  (Rule 130). The picker has no `S`.

## Not done yet

- `F` (sync) and the cache it would own: every preview, creation and scan
  refetches.
- A private git repository on a host that is not the forge's is fetched
  anonymously, so it fails with git's own reason: use an SSH URL.
- No spinner on the row itself: the footer status carries the live scan.

Deux approches possibles, et le choix dépend d'un point technique que DevDesk tranche déjà pour toi.

**Option recommandée — un seul repo git, plusieurs entrées `git` avec des `Path` différents**

Dans `~/.devdesk/templates.yaml`, une entrée par template :
```yaml
- slug: go-http-api
  source: {kind: git, url: git@github.com:toi/templates.git, path: go/http-api, ref: v1.2.0}
- slug: node-express
  source: {kind: git, url: git@github.com:toi/templates.git, path: node/express, ref: v1.2.0}
```
Même repo, même URL, `path` = le sous-dossier de l'arborescence langage/framework, `ref` = un tag figé (pas `main`, sinon un template change sous les repos déjà créés avec).

Pas besoin de clone local : DevDesk fait un `git init` + `fetch --depth 1 <ref>` + `archive` à chaque usage (`internal/template/fetch.go:100`). Ça ne prend que ce qui est **committé** — pas de `.git`, pas de fichiers ignorés, pas de modifs non commitées, symlinks et submodules refusés explicitement. Pas encore de cache (le sync `F` est prévu mais pas fait), donc chaque preview/scan/création refetch.

**Ton idée — clone local + référence sur disque (`kind: local`)**

Ça existe (`Source.Kind: local`, `Path` = répertoire du repo), mais **actuellement ça ne prend pas de sous-dossier** — `fetch.go:107` appelle `git.ArchiveLocal` avec un sous-chemin vide en dur, contrairement au `kind: git` distant qui, lui, accepte un `Path`. Donc avec une seule arborescence multi-langages clonée une fois, chaque entrée `local` récupérerait **tout le repo**, pas le sous-dossier voulu.

Pour que ton schéma marche avec `local`, il faudrait soit :
- cloner un checkout séparé par langage/framework (perd l'intérêt du repo unique), soit
- étendre `KindLocal` pour accepter un `Path` de sous-dossier comme `KindGit` (petit changement dans `internal/template/fetch.go` + `template.go` + le formulaire `:templates`).

Sauf besoin de travailler hors-ligne, je partirais sur la première option : un seul repo distant, une entrée par sous-dossier, tags pour figer les versions.

3	import (

13	// toolCmd is one subprocess invocation: the binary and the arguments handed to
14	// it. Building it is pure, which is what makes the argument surface — the part
15	// that decides what a scanner is actually asked to do — testable without a
16	// scanner installed.
17	//
18	// It is also what the UI displays. Deriving the shown command and the executed
19	// one from the same value is the point: the two used to be built separately and
20	// had drifted (§1.3 D19).
21	type toolCmd struct {
22		Name string
23		Args []string
24		// Env is the child's whole environment when it is not nil, os.Environ()
25		// plus what the caller added. It exists so a credential can reach a tool
26		// without going through argv, which is readable from the process list —
27		// the arrangement the clone already uses for http.extraHeader (§3.16).
28		//
29		// String() never renders it: the invocation is logged and shown in the UI.
30		Env []string
31	
32		// Dir is the working directory the tool runs in, when it has one.
33		//
34		// It exists for plumber, whose `analyze` takes **no path argument**: it
35		// works on the current directory. Without this the tool ran in whatever
36		// directory DevDesk was launched from and reported
37		// `--project is required (could not auto-detect from git remote)` — a
38		// failure about a repository nobody had asked it to look at. Trivy and
39		// Gitleaks take their target in argv and set nothing here.
40		Dir string
41	}
42	
43	// String renders the invocation as a shell command line, for logs and for the
44	// command the UI shows next to a scan.
45	func (c toolCmd) String() string {
46		if c.Name == "" {
47			return ""
48		}
49		line := strings.Join(append([]string{c.Name}, c.Args...), " ")
50		// The directory is part of what the command means when the tool takes no
51		// path: a logged invocation that cannot be re-run says less than it looks
52		// like it does.
53		if c.Dir != "" {
54			return "cd " + c.Dir + " && " + line
55		}
56		return line
57	}
58	
59	// exitError reports a tool that ran and exited non-zero. The code matters:
60	// both scanners use a non-zero exit to mean "I found something" rather than
61	// "I failed" — trivy for vulnerabilities, gitleaks for secrets — so callers
62	// have to tell the two apart.
63	type exitError struct {
64		Code   int
65		Stderr string
66	}
67	
68	func (e *exitError) Error() string {
69		if e.Stderr != "" {
70			return fmt.Sprintf("exit status %d: %s", e.Code, strings.TrimSpace(e.Stderr))
71		}
72		return fmt.Sprintf("exit status %d", e.Code)
73	}
74	
75	// commandRunner is the seam every subprocess in this package passes through.
76	//
77	// The package drives trivy and gitleaks as external processes, which makes it
78	// untestable without both installed and a repository to point them at. Routing
79	// through this interface lets tests exercise the argument building, the
80	// exit-code handling and the output parsing — where the defects live — against
81	// canned output.
82	type commandRunner interface {
83		// Run executes tc and returns what it wrote to stdout. Lines written to
84		// stderr are forwarded to progressFn as they arrive, which is how Trivy
85		// reports its database download. A tool that runs and exits non-zero
86		// returns its stdout along with an *exitError.
87		Run(ctx context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]byte, error)
88	}
89	
90	// cliRunner is the production commandRunner: it shells out to the real tools.
91	type cliRunner struct{}
92	
93	func (cliRunner) Run(ctx context.Context, tc toolCmd, progressFn func(string)) ([]byte, error) {
94		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, tc.Name, tc.Args...) //nolint:gosec // name is one of trivy/gitleaks/plumber/docker
95		cmd.Env = tc.Env                                     // nil inherits this process's environment, which is the default
96		cmd.Dir = tc.Dir                                     // empty runs in DevDesk's own working directory
97	
98		var stdout bytes.Buffer
99		cmd.Stdout = &stdout
100	
101		// Stderr is consumed two ways: streamed to progressFn while the tool runs,
102		// and kept so a failure can be reported with the tool's own diagnostic.
103		var stderr bytes.Buffer
104		if progressFn != nil {
105			pipe, err := cmd.StderrPipe()
106			if err == nil {
107				done := make(chan struct{})
108				go func() {
109					defer close(done)
110					sc := bufio.NewScanner(pipe)
111					for sc.Scan() {
112						line := strings.TrimSpace(sc.Text())
113						if line == "" {
114							continue
115						}
116						stderr.WriteString(line)
117						stderr.WriteByte('\n')
118						progressFn(line)
119					}
120					// A read failure on the progress pipe is not a scan failure:
121					// the report comes back on stdout, and the tool's exit code
122					// says whether it succeeded. Dropping the rest of the progress
123					// is the whole consequence.
124					_ = sc.Err()
125				}()
126				if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
127					return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s failed to start: %w", tc.Name, err)
128				}
129				<-done // drain stderr before Wait closes the pipe
130				return finish(tc.Name, cmd, &stdout, &stderr)
131			}
132		}
133	
134		cmd.Stderr = &stderr
135		if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil {
136			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s failed to start: %w", tc.Name, err)
137		}
138		return finish(tc.Name, cmd, &stdout, &stderr)
139	}
140	
141	// finish waits for the tool and only then reads what it wrote.
142	//
143	// The order is the point, and it is not a style preference: os/exec fills the
144	// output buffers from goroutines it owns, and only Wait guarantees they are
145	// done. Reading the buffer in the same expression as Wait — which is what
146	// `return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(..., cmd.Wait(), ...)` does, since operands
147	// are evaluated before the call — snapshots it while it is still empty, and
148	// every scan comes back with no findings.
149	func finish(name string, cmd *exec.Cmd, stdout, stderr *bytes.Buffer) ([]byte, error) {
150		err := cmd.Wait()
151		return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(name, err, stderr.String())
152	}
153	
154	// waitErr turns a non-zero exit into an *exitError carrying the code, and
155	// leaves anything else (a killed process, a broken pipe) as it is.
156	func waitErr(name string, err error, stderr string) error {
157		if err == nil {
158			return nil
159		}
160		var exitErr *exec.ExitError
161		if errors.As(err, &exitErr) {
162			if stderr == "" {
163				stderr = string(exitErr.Stderr)
164			}
165			return &exitError{Code: exitErr.ExitCode(), Stderr: stderr}
166		}
167		return fmt.Errorf("%s failed: %w", name, err)
168	}

171	// package stays safe to call concurrently; tests that swap it must not run in
172	// parallel.
